implementation_notes: Enumerable puts the whole operation set on every collection: the documentation lists map (aliased as collect), find_all (aliased select/filter), reject, flat_map, filter_map and grep for selection and transformation, plus inject (aliased reduce) 'when you want to reduce a collection to a single value', along with group_by, each_with_object, sum and sort_by. Blocks and &:symbol replace hand-written loops; the chain is eager, which keeps every step inspectable and makes it the default form.
code_sketch:
emails = people
  .select(&:active?)
  .map(&:email)
  .uniq
  .sort
  .first(10)

total = orders.sum(&:amount)                                # terminal (Ruby 2.4+)
named = orders.inject(0) { |sum, o| sum + o.amount }        # classic reduce
pitfalls: The chain is eager: every step allocates an intermediate Array, so large inputs need #lazy or each_with_object instead.
&:symbol shorthand only works for zero-arity methods, and blocks with side effects run once per element even when the result is discarded.
Hash iteration passes [key, value] pairs to single-parameter blocks, which silently changes what a map/select block sees unless it destructures.

variants.name: Enumerator::Lazy chain
variants.implementation_notes: #lazy returns an Enumerator::Lazy, which the documentation describes as 'a special type of Enumerator, that allows constructing chains of operations without evaluating them immediately' - it redefines most Enumerable methods so they just build another lazy enumerator, so no intermediate arrays are created and the chain enumerates only as far as the consumer needs. Force it with #force/#to_a or a short-circuiting terminal (first/take/find). The same documentation warns that lazy map/select need an explicit block (a block-less call raises ArgumentError) and that the real enumeration happens only when a non-redefined method is called.
pitfalls: A lazy chain without a terminal does nothing, and Enumerator::Lazy#map without a block raises ArgumentError where the eager version would return an Enumerator.
Laziness makes debugging harder and re-runs upstream work on each traversal; side effects in the chain now happen at consumer-driven times.
